task: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. In about 9% of conversations the agent tells the customer "Let me pull up your order" and then nothing else happens; no refund is issued. Logs show the last API response in those cases had stop_reason "tool_use". Here is the loop:

```python
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=4096,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.content[0].type == "text":
        return resp.content[0].text
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
```

What is the root cause and the correct fix?

options.A: The first block's type is not a stop signal; branch on stop_reason, continuing on "tool_use" and returning on "end_turn".
options.B: Claude writes text before some tool calls; instruct it in the system prompt never to emit text in a response that contains a tool call.
options.C: The loop should scan the returned text for phrases like "let me" or "one moment" and keep iterating whenever it finds one.
options.D: The loop has no turn limit; add a maximum of 10 iterations so a stalled conversation is cut off and passed to a human agent.

rationale: Claude can emit explanatory text and a tool_use block in the same response, so the first block's type says nothing about whether work remains. stop_reason is the authoritative signal: "tool_use" means execute and continue, "end_turn" means finished. A turn cap (D) is a safety net that would not fix the premature exit. A prompt rule (B) is probabilistic and still leaves the wrong signal in code. Scanning text for phrases (C) is the natural-language parsing anti-pattern.
evidence: Loop control should key off stop_reason (tool_use vs end_turn), not off text content or the first block type.

task: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. After a customer message about a late package, the agent crashes with a 400 on its second request. Trace:

```text
POST /v1/messages -> 200  stop_reason=tool_use
  content: [text, tool_use get_customer (toolu_01A),
            tool_use lookup_order (toolu_01B)]
loop: executed toolu_01A -> ok
loop: appended user message [tool_result toolu_01A]
POST /v1/messages -> 400 invalid_request_error
  "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks
   immediately after: toolu_01B"
```

What change to the loop fixes this class of failure?

options.A: Raise max_tokens so the response is not cut off before the model has finished writing its second tool call.
options.B: Run every tool_use block in the assistant message and return all of the tool_result blocks together in one user message.
options.C: Treat the 400 as transient and retry the identical request with exponential backoff and jitter.
options.D: Send the lookup_order result in a second user message immediately after the one holding the get_customer result.

rationale: The assistant message contained two tool_use blocks, and the API requires a matching tool_result for each in the very next user message. Executing all blocks and returning all results together satisfies that for any number of parallel calls. A 400 is not retryable (C), and the identical request would fail again. Splitting results across two user messages (D) still leaves the first message incomplete. The content shows both blocks arrived intact, so truncation (A) is not involved.
evidence: Parallel tool calls: return all tool_result blocks in a single user message; 400 errors are not retryable.

task: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Your search subagent uses a server-side web search tool and loops while stop_reason is "tool_use", treating anything else as final. In about 7% of runs the coordinator receives only a one-line preamble ("I'll search for recent regulatory filings...") and no findings. Logs show those responses ended with stop_reason "pause_turn". How should the subagent loop handle this?

options.A: Return the preamble as the result, and have the coordinator re-delegate the same search to a fresh subagent.
options.B: On pause_turn, send the response back as the assistant turn in a new request so the turn continues.
options.C: Raise max_tokens so the server-side search finishes inside a single response and never pauses at all.
options.D: Add a line to the subagent prompt telling it to complete every search within a single response without pausing.

rationale: pause_turn means a long-running server-side turn was paused; the documented handling is to pass the response back so Claude resumes where it stopped. A larger max_tokens (C) addresses max_tokens truncation, a different stop reason. Re-delegating (A) discards progress and may pause again. A prompt instruction (D) cannot control a server-side pause. The lesson: handle every stop_reason explicitly instead of equating non-tool_use with done.
evidence: pause_turn: resume by sending the response back as-is; check stop_reason before reading content.

task: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A teammate's codebase-exploration agent, built directly on the Messages API, behaves erratically: it sometimes stops mid-investigation and sometimes repeats greps it already ran. Reviewing the loop, you find it (1) ends when the reply text contains "Investigation complete", (2) caps at 8 iterations, and (3) sends only the most recent tool result in each new request. Which TWO changes make the loop correct? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Terminate when stop_reason is "end_turn" instead of matching marker text in the reply.
options.B: Lower the iteration cap from 8 to 5 so the agent has fewer chances to repeat the same grep.
options.C: Start every iteration with a fresh message list containing a one-paragraph summary the agent wrote itself.
options.D: Ask Claude to put a "status": "done" field in its prose and parse that field to decide when to stop.
options.E: Append each assistant message and its tool results to the history so Claude sees everything gathered so far.

rationale: Termination should come from stop_reason, and continuity comes from accumulating the assistant turns and tool_result blocks so the model can reason about what it has already found. Lowering the cap (B) only truncates work and is not a stopping mechanism. A status field in prose (D) is still a natural-language completion signal. Rebuilding context from an agent-written summary each turn (C) drops the raw results that the next decision depends on.
evidence: Continue on tool_use, stop on end_turn, and append tool results to history; avoid text-based completion signals and arbitrary caps.

task: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Query logs show 68% of requests are single-fact lookups such as "When did the EU AI Act enter into force?", yet the coordinator always runs the search, analysis, synthesis, and report subagents in sequence. Median latency is three minutes. Answers to complex, multi-source questions are good and must not regress. How should you cut latency?

options.A: Merge the four subagents into one agent holding every tool, so the whole pipeline runs in a single context.
options.B: Run the analysis and synthesis subagents at the same time as search so the stages overlap in wall-clock time.
options.C: Have the coordinator assess each query and invoke only the subagents it needs, such as search alone for a single-fact lookup.
options.D: Place a separate classifier service ahead of the coordinator that sends simple queries to a standalone search-only application.

rationale: A coordinator is meant to analyze query requirements and choose which subagents to invoke rather than push every request through the full pipeline. Merging everything (A) gives up the context isolation that keeps complex runs good. An external classifier (D) adds a layer and a second system to maintain for a decision the coordinator can already make. Analysis and synthesis (B) depend on search output, so they cannot meaningfully overlap with it.
evidence: Coordinators should dynamically select subagents by query complexity instead of always running the full pipeline.

task: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A report on EU battery regulation cites 14 sources, all trade press. Reviewers expected regulator filings and supplier disclosures. Logs show all three search subagents received the same delegation prompt ("research EU battery regulation") and returned heavily overlapping articles. Which TWO changes best address the coverage gap and the duplication? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Give each search subagent a distinct source type or subtopic in its delegation prompt: press, regulator filings, supplier disclosures.
options.B: Raise each search subagent's result limit from 10 to 50 so that more source types surface by chance.
options.C: Have the coordinator review the synthesis output for gaps and re-delegate targeted queries before the report is finalized.
options.D: Switch the synthesis subagent to a larger model so it can infer what the missing source types would have said.
options.E: Let the three search subagents message each other during their runs so they can deduplicate results themselves.

rationale: Partitioning scope by subtopic or source type removes the duplication at its origin, and a coordinator-driven refinement loop catches remaining gaps and sends targeted follow-up queries. A bigger synthesis model (D) cannot create evidence that was never retrieved. Peer messaging (E) bypasses the coordinator, which should own communication, error handling, and observability. More results per identical prompt (B) mostly yields more of the same press coverage.
evidence: Partition research scope across subagents and use coordinator-led refinement loops to fill gaps.

task: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The coordinator ran the search and document-analysis subagents, then delegated to synthesis as shown. The synthesis subagent replies that it has nothing to work with.

```text
coordinator -> Agent(subagent_type="synthesis",
  prompt="Synthesize the findings from the search and analysis
          agents into a two-page brief with citations.")

synthesis -> "I don't have any findings. Please provide the
              search and analysis results."
```

What is the correct fix?

options.A: Include the complete findings in the synthesis prompt as structured records that keep each claim apart from its source URL, document name, and page.
options.B: Resume the search subagent's session from inside the synthesis subagent so it can read that agent's earlier transcript.
options.C: Tell the synthesis subagent in its prompt to re-run the web searches itself and rebuild the findings before writing.
options.D: Write the findings into the synthesis AgentDefinition's system prompt when the coordinator application is configured.

rationale: Subagents start with a fresh context and receive only what the coordinator puts in the delegation prompt, so the findings must be passed explicitly. Structured records preserve attribution so citations survive synthesis. Sessions are not shared between subagents (B). An AgentDefinition is static (D) and cannot hold results produced at runtime. Re-running searches (C) duplicates work and may return different sources than the ones analyzed.
evidence: Subagents do not inherit parent context; the only channel is the prompt string, so findings and attribution must be included.

task: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The three search subagents are independent of one another, but the search phase is slow. Trace from one run:

```text
t=0s    coordinator    Agent(search-news)      launched
t=62s   search-news    returned 9 findings
t=63s   coordinator    Agent(search-filings)   launched
t=118s  search-filings returned 6 findings
t=119s  coordinator    Agent(search-academic)  launched
t=171s  search-academic returned 11 findings
t=172s  coordinator    Agent(synthesis)        launched
```

What change brings the search phase close to the duration of the slowest single search?

options.A: Switch the three search subagents to a smaller, faster model tier while keeping the one-per-turn delegation.
options.B: Have each search subagent hand its findings to the next one in its prompt so later searches start with warm context.
options.C: Raise the concurrent-subagent limit for the session from its default to 40 so more subagents are allowed to run at once.
options.D: Have the coordinator issue all three Agent tool calls in a single response so the subagents run concurrently.

rationale: Each search was launched in its own coordinator turn, so they ran back to back (62 + 55 + 52 seconds). Emitting multiple Agent calls in one response lets them run concurrently. The concurrency limit (C) was never reached; only one subagent was ever running. A faster model (A) shortens each step but leaves the sequential structure. Chaining findings (B) makes the dependency explicit and does nothing to remove it.
evidence: Spawn parallel subagents by emitting multiple Agent (Task) tool calls in a single coordinator response.

task: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. You deploy this coordinator headless, with no interactive approver. It never delegates: its attempts to call a subagent come back as denied tool calls, and it falls back to searching the web by itself.

```python
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["WebSearch", "Read"],
    agents={
        "search": AgentDefinition(description="Finds sources on a topic",
                                  prompt=SEARCH_PROMPT, tools=["WebSearch"]),
        "synthesis": AgentDefinition(description="Merges findings into a brief",
                                     prompt=SYNTH_PROMPT, tools=["Read"]),
    },
)
```

What is the fix?

options.A: Add the subagent-spawning tool, Agent (formerly Task), to the coordinator's allowed_tools.
options.B: Move the two definitions into .claude/agents/ files so the coordinator can discover them at startup time.
options.C: Rewrite both descriptions to say the coordinator must delegate to the agent for every request.
options.D: Add Read and WebSearch to the search definition's tools list so it can finish the work itself.

rationale: Subagents are invoked through the Agent tool (called Task in older versions). With no approver, a call to a tool that is not in allowed_tools is denied, so the coordinator never delegates. Better descriptions (C) help Claude choose a subagent but cannot grant the missing permission. File-based definitions (B) change where agents are defined, not whether the coordinator may call the tool. Widening a subagent's tools (D) is unrelated to the denied delegation.
evidence: Claude invokes subagents through the Agent tool (formerly Task); it must be permitted in the coordinator's allowed tools.

task: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. When the agent calls escalate_to_human for a policy exception, human agents in the ticketing system see only the fields passed in the tool call and cannot open the conversation transcript. They report spending several minutes re-asking customers what they already told Claude. Which THREE fields should the escalate_to_human payload include? (Select THREE.)

options.A: The recommended next action for the human agent.
options.B: The model's step-by-step reasoning from every turn of the conversation.
options.C: The root cause of the problem and the refund amount at stake.
options.D: The verified customer ID and the order or orders involved.
options.E: Every raw tool response returned by the backend during the session.

rationale: A human who cannot see the transcript needs a compact, structured summary: who the customer is, what went wrong and what is owed, and what Claude recommends. Dumping reasoning from every turn (B) or all raw tool output (E) recreates the transcript-reading problem the summary is meant to remove and buries the decision-relevant facts.
evidence: Handoff summaries for humans without transcript access should carry customer ID, root cause, amount, and recommended action.

task: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. In 11% of conversations where the customer writes "transfer me to a person", the agent replies with troubleshooting steps first, and those customers rate the interaction poorly. Most of these cases are within the agent's authority (damaged item with photo attached). Which change best fixes the behavior?

options.A: Add an explicit rule with examples: if the customer asks for a human, call escalate_to_human at once with a handoff summary.
options.B: Have the agent report a confidence score from 1 to 10 each turn and escalate automatically below a fixed cutoff.
options.C: Add sentiment scoring on each customer message and escalate when the frustration score passes a set threshold.
options.D: Resolve the issue first when it is within the agent's authority, then offer a transfer in the closing message of the chat.

rationale: An explicit request for a human is a defined escalation trigger and should be honored immediately, with the handoff context attached, even when the agent could solve the problem. Resolving first (D) overrides the customer's stated choice. Sentiment (C) and self-reported confidence (B) are unreliable proxies for what the customer asked for, and neither detects an explicit request.
evidence: Escalate immediately when a customer explicitly requests a human; sentiment and self-reported confidence are poor proxies.

task: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Policy: refunds over $500 must be escalated. The hook below is registered, yet logs show a $740 refund went through. No hook_callback_failed message appears in the message stream.

```python
async def cap_refund(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    if input_data["tool_input"].get("amount", 0) > 500:
        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
            "permissionDecision": "deny",
            "permissionDecisionReason": "Over $500: call escalate_to_human."}}
    return {}

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    mcp_servers={"support": support_server},
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="process_refund", hooks=[cap_refund])]})

# log: tool_use name=mcp__support__process_refund amount=740 -> ok
```

Why did the refund go through, and what fixes it?

options.A: The matcher misses the namespaced MCP name; match mcp__support__process_refund or a pattern like ^mcp__support__.
options.B: Set on_failure="block" on the matcher so that a callback that fails stops the refund from being processed at all.
options.C: The check must run in a PostToolUse hook, because the amount is only reliable after the tool has returned its result.
options.D: The matcher should be removed so that the hook runs for every event type, including events that fire after the tool executes.

rationale: MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, and matchers test the tool name, so the bare "process_refund" pattern never selects this call and the callback never runs. Fixing the matcher makes the deterministic deny take effect and redirects to escalation. A PostToolUse check (C) would run after the money has moved. Dropping the matcher (D) misses the point that it is the name pattern that is wrong. on_failure="block" (B) only matters when a callback throws, and none did here.
evidence: Tool-hook matchers test the tool name; MCP tools use the mcp__<server>__<action> pattern; PreToolUse can deny.

task: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your triage agent uses three MCP servers that your vendor owns. The CI server returns finished_at as Unix seconds (1730678400), the issue tracker returns ISO 8601 strings, and the deploy tool returns status as integers (0, 1, 2). In 8% of triage runs the agent misorders events or misreports deploy state. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add few-shot examples that show epoch timestamps and status integers being converted correctly.
options.B: Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each result into ISO 8601 timestamps and named statuses before the model reads it.
options.C: Document each server's formats in the system prompt and ask the agent to convert all values to one format before comparing them.
options.D: Fork each vendor MCP server and change its output format so that all three servers agree with one another.

rationale: A PostToolUse hook runs in your code on every result, so the model only ever sees one consistent format, and it works without touching vendor servers. Prompt instructions (C) and few-shot examples (A) ask the model to do deterministic conversion work and still fail some fraction of the time. Forking vendor servers (D) creates a maintenance burden for something a thin hook layer does.
evidence: PostToolUse hooks can normalize heterogeneous formats (timestamps, status codes) before the model processes results.

task: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. After a long session mapping the payments module (about 80 tool calls), you want to prototype two refactors, extracting a service and an event-driven design, without paying for that analysis twice. Both prototypes will edit the same files. Which TWO actions fit? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Start two new sessions and have each one re-explore the module before it begins its refactor.
options.B: Resume the original session and ask for both refactors one after the other so the second can learn from the first.
options.C: Fork the analysis session once per approach so each branch starts from the same history.
options.D: Enable plan mode in the original session and write both designs into the same plan file.
options.E: Give each branch its own git worktree, since a fork copies conversation history but not the files on disk.

rationale: Forking gives two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, and separate worktrees keep their file edits from colliding because forks branch only the conversation. Sequential work in one session (B) contaminates the second design with the first. Fresh sessions (A) repeat the 80-call exploration you wanted to avoid. A shared plan file (D) merges the designs instead of keeping them independent.
evidence: Fork branches conversation history from a shared baseline; it does not branch the filesystem.

task: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Yesterday you named a session "billing-audit" after Claude mapped 140 files. Overnight a teammate merged a refactor that renamed functions in three of them (invoice.py, tax.py, ledger.py). Resumed today, Claude still cites the old function names. The rest of the analysis remains valid. What is the most efficient way to continue?

options.A: Resume the named session and tell Claude which three files changed so it re-reads only those.
options.B: Resume the session and ask Claude to re-verify its whole earlier analysis against the current repository.
options.C: Fork the resumed session, assuming a fork re-reads changed files automatically.
options.D: Discard the session and start a new one with the original prompt, re-exploring all 140 files from scratch.

rationale: The prior context is mostly valid, so resuming keeps most of the work, and naming the changed files enables targeted re-analysis instead of full re-exploration. Re-verifying everything (B) spends tokens on 137 unchanged files. Starting over (D) discards valid analysis. A fork (C) copies the same stale history and does not re-read files on its own.
evidence: When resuming after code changes, inform the agent of specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than full re-exploration.

task: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A legacy 400-file Python service has no tests, and leadership asks for "comprehensive tests". A developer scripts a loop that walks files alphabetically and asks Claude to write tests for each. Early output covers trivial utilities while the billing and auth modules remain untested. What is the better decomposition?

options.A: Keep the per-file loop, but sort the files by size so the largest modules are handled first in each run.
options.B: Add a 90% coverage threshold per file to the loop script and retry any file that falls below that target.
options.C: Ask Claude in one prompt to write tests for the whole repository and then review the combined output afterwards.
options.D: Map structure in plan mode, rank modules by risk and impact, then follow a prioritized plan that adapts.

rationale: Open-ended work like this benefits from adaptive decomposition: first map the codebase, find high-impact areas, then build and revise a prioritized plan as dependencies are discovered. Sorting by size (A) is still a fixed order that ignores risk. One giant prompt (C) overloads attention and context. A coverage gate (B) measures lines hit, not whether the riskiest modules were prioritized, and it keeps the arbitrary order.
evidence: Decompose open-ended tasks by mapping structure, identifying high-impact areas, then creating a prioritized plan that adapts.

task: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK maintenance agent runs shell commands through the Bash tool, including database migrations. Policy: any migration or DROP against a shared environment needs a human to approve it first. The system prompt already says "ask before irreversible commands", yet one run migrated the shared staging database without asking. How should you enforce the policy?

options.A: Add a PostToolUse hook on Bash that notifies the team in chat after any migration command finishes running.
options.B: Move the approval sentence to the top of the system prompt and add two examples of correct approval requests for risky steps.
options.C: Remove Bash and leave the agent with read-only tools so that it cannot run migrations of any kind.
options.D: Register a PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command and returns "ask" or "deny" for migration and DROP patterns.

rationale: A PreToolUse hook runs outside the model before the command executes and can force a human approval or a denial for matching commands, giving a deterministic checkpoint. Prompt text and examples (B) are probabilistic and already failed once. A PostToolUse notification (A) arrives after the migration has run. Removing Bash (C) is over-engineered and breaks the agent's legitimate maintenance work.
evidence: PreToolUse hooks can deny or require approval deterministically; prompt-only enforcement has a non-zero failure rate.

task: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your team runs two CI jobs. Job 1 reviews every PR for the same three aspects: security, test coverage, and API-doc updates. Job 2 investigates nightly flaky-test failures whose root causes vary: races, dependency drift, shared fixtures, infrastructure outages. A fixed three-step chain works for Job 1 but often misses the cause in Job 2. How should Job 2 be restructured?

options.A: Let the agent derive subtasks from what each step finds: map failing tests, classify patterns, then dig into the main cluster.
options.B: Run the existing three-step chain three times and keep only the findings that appear in at least two of the runs.
options.C: Extend the fixed chain to eight steps covering every root cause seen so far in the incident history, including infrastructure outages.
options.D: Give each failing test its own independent single-pass job and merge the separate outputs at the end of the run.

rationale: Job 1 is predictable, which suits prompt chaining. Job 2 is open-ended: what to examine next depends on what the previous step discovered, so subtasks should be generated adaptively. A longer fixed chain (C) only encodes past causes. Voting across identical runs (B) repeats the same blind spots. Isolated per-test jobs (D) cannot see cross-test patterns such as a shared fixture.
evidence: Use prompt chaining for predictable multi-aspect work and adaptive decomposition for open-ended investigation.

task: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A CI auto-fix job must never modify workflow files. You added the hook below, but a run still rewrote .github/workflows/deploy.yml, and the job log shows the hook's message in stderr.

```json
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
               "command": ".claude/hooks/protect-workflows.sh" } ] } ] } }
```
```bash
path=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')
if [[ "$path" == *".github/workflows/"* ]]; then
  echo "Workflow files are off limits in CI." >&2
  exit 1
fi
```

What is wrong?

options.A: The matcher is applied to file paths, so it must be changed to "*" before the hook can see workflow file edits at all.
options.B: The check should run in PostToolUse and revert the file whenever the path matches a workflow file.
options.C: Exit code 1 is non-blocking; exit with code 2 or print a JSON deny decision so the edit is actually blocked.
options.D: The rule belongs in CLAUDE.md, because settings hooks only record events and cannot affect any tool calls.

rationale: The hook ran (stderr shows its message) and detected the path, but for command hooks only exit code 2, or a JSON deny decision, blocks the tool call; other non-zero codes are treated as non-blocking errors. Matchers test tool names (A), and Edit|Write already matches. Hooks can block calls, so moving the rule to CLAUDE.md (D) would weaken it to a suggestion. A PostToolUse revert (B) lets the edit happen first and is not preventive.
evidence: In Claude Code command hooks, exit code 2 blocks a tool call; other non-zero exits do not.

task: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A review coordinator fans out to security, test, and dependency reviewer subagents. When the dependency reviewer timed out on a large monorepo PR, it returned an empty findings list, and the coordinator posted "No issues found" and set the check to passed. Which TWO changes fix the failure handling? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Retry inside the subagent with exponential backoff, returning an empty list if every attempt fails.
options.B: Have the coordinator mark the check incomplete and list unreviewed scope whenever a subagent reports a failure.
options.C: Abort the whole CI job on any subagent error and discard the other reviewers' findings entirely.
options.D: Raise the dependency reviewer's timeout to 30 minutes so that empty results cannot occur on large pull requests.
options.E: Have each subagent return a structured status: failure type, scope not reviewed, and any partial findings.

rationale: The root problem is that a failure looked like a success. A structured error with partial results lets the coordinator tell the difference and decide how to recover, and an explicit incomplete status keeps a silent gap from reading as a pass. A longer timeout (D) only delays the next failure. An empty list after retries (A) is the same silent success. Aborting everything (C) throws away valid findings from the two healthy reviewers.
evidence: Propagate structured error context (failure type, scope, partial results) so the coordinator can recover; do not mask failures as empty success.

task: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Contracts average 60 pages and the schema has 40 fields spread across sections. A single-pass extraction call fills most fields but skips some clauses and, in about 10% of documents, returns a renewal term that conflicts with an amendment in the annex. How should you decompose the work?

options.A: Extract per section in focused passes, then run a separate pass that reconciles conflicts such as amendments overriding base terms.
options.B: Run the single-pass call three times and take the majority value for each field, flagging for human review any fields where the runs disagree.
options.C: Add the 40 field definitions and one fully worked example contract to the prompt of the single-pass call.
options.D: Split the document into fixed 10-page chunks, extract each one, and concatenate the resulting JSON arrays.

rationale: Splitting into focused local passes avoids attention dilution, and a separate integration pass handles the cross-section reasoning (an annex amendment overriding a base term) that no local pass can see. Majority voting (B) repeats the same blind spots. Fixed page chunks (D) cut clauses at arbitrary boundaries and still never reconcile conflicts. A richer prompt (C) leaves the single pass overloaded.
evidence: Split large analyses into per-unit local passes plus a separate cross-unit integration pass.

task: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. About 3% of invoice records land in the warehouse with a null line-items array. A trace of one such run:

```text
POST /v1/messages -> 200
  stop_reason=max_tokens  usage.output_tokens=4096
  content[0].text='{"invoice_id":"INV-8841","lines":[{"sku":"A12","qty":3,
    "price":19.5},{"sku":"B07","qty":'
pipeline: json.loads -> JSONDecodeError
pipeline: except -> save record, lines=null, status=ok
```

What is the correct fix?

options.A: Check stop_reason before parsing; on max_tokens, re-request with a larger max_tokens (streamed) or split the document, and never store partial output.
options.B: Add a repair step that closes open brackets and quotes so the truncated JSON parses and keeps the lines it did capture.
options.C: Add "keep every invoice response under 4000 tokens" to the prompt so the output fits within the existing limit.
options.D: Retry the identical request on JSONDecodeError with exponential backoff until the response parses cleanly.

rationale: stop_reason "max_tokens" means the response was cut off, so it is incomplete rather than final, and parsing it silently loses data. The pipeline must branch on stop_reason and either raise the limit or reduce the work per call. Repairing truncated JSON (B) fabricates a plausible-looking but incomplete record. A length instruction (C) is probabilistic against a hard limit. An identical retry (D) hits the same ceiling every time.
evidence: Check stop_reason before reading content; max_tokens means a truncated response.

task: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. An overnight agent session extracting 500 vendor PDFs crashed at document 312. Each extracted record is already saved in a database keyed by document ID. Meanwhile finance re-uploaded corrected versions of about 20 of the first 311 documents, and the crashed transcript holds roughly 600K tokens of tool results. What is the more reliable recovery?

options.A: Resume the crashed session and instruct it to disregard any earlier tool results for the 20 re-uploaded documents.
options.B: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of completed IDs and results, then process the 20 replaced and the 189 remaining documents.
options.C: Fork the crashed session at document 311 and run the remaining documents in the forked branch.
options.D: Resume the crashed session so the earlier results stay in context, and continue from document 312 onward.

rationale: When prior tool results are stale (20 documents changed) and the transcript is huge, a fresh session with an injected structured summary is more reliable than resuming, and the database already holds the durable state. Resuming (D) carries stale results and a bloated context forward. Telling the resumed agent to ignore some results (A) leaves them in context and depends on the model complying. A fork (C) copies the same stale history.
evidence: Starting fresh with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results.

task: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your pipeline has invoice-extraction, contract-extraction, and validation subagents. To save a hop, the validation subagent calls the extraction subagents directly to re-extract failed fields. In production some documents cycle between extraction and validation dozens of times, and the logs do not show which subagent retried what. Which architecture change is best?

options.A: Route re-extraction requests through the coordinator, which owns retry limits, error handling, and logging.
options.B: Add a shared retry counter variable that every subagent reads and increments before it calls another subagent in the pipeline.
options.C: Keep the direct calls, but have the validation subagent append each retry to a log file for later offline analysis.
options.D: Merge validation into each extraction subagent so that no handoff between subagents is needed at all in production.

rationale: In a hub-and-spoke design the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, which gives one place for retry limits, consistent error handling, and observability. A shared counter (B) and a side log (C) bolt monitoring onto a topology that still hides control flow from the coordinator. Merging validation into each extractor (D) removes the independent check and duplicates validation logic.
evidence: Route all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.

task: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Two developers on one repository get different behavior: Priya's sessions always use pnpm, while Marcus's sessions keep running npm install. This is the memory listing from Priya's machine:

```text
/memory (Priya)
  user     ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md   "Use pnpm, never npm. Run pnpm lint before every commit."
  project  ./CLAUDE.md           "Services live under /services. Tests: pnpm test."
  local    ./CLAUDE.local.md     "Sandbox API: https://sandbox.internal:8443"
```

The team wants every current and future contributor to follow the pnpm rule with no per-person setup. What should you change?

options.A: Add an @~/.claude/CLAUDE.md import to the project CLAUDE.md so each session pulls in the user-level file as well.
options.B: Move the pnpm and lint rules into the committed ./CLAUDE.md, so that every clone loads them as shared project instructions.
options.C: Copy the pnpm and lint rules into ./CLAUDE.local.md and commit that file so it ships with the repository clone.
options.D: Deploy the rules as a managed-policy CLAUDE.md in /etc/claude-code on each developer laptop through the company's device-management tooling.

rationale: The rule sits in Priya's user-level file, which exists only on her machine, so Marcus never receives it. Project instructions that must reach every contributor belong in the committed ./CLAUDE.md (B). An @ import of a home-directory file (A) points at a file teammates do not have. CLAUDE.local.md (C) is the personal, gitignored layer; committing it defeats its purpose and mixes private sandbox URLs into the repo. A managed-policy file (D) is an organization-wide mechanism that needs per-machine deployment, which is far more than a single repository's convention requires.
evidence: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and not shared; project-level ./CLAUDE.md is committed and loaded for everyone who works in the repo.

task: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A platform team keeps its Terraform conventions in `.claude/rules/terraform.md`, but Claude ignores them in nested modules. Edits to infra/main.tf load the rule; edits to infra/modules/vpc/main.tf do not. The rule's frontmatter:

```yaml
---
paths:
  - "infra/*.tf"
---
```

What is the cause?

options.A: The single `*` stops at directory boundaries, so only files directly in infra/ match; use `infra/**/*.tf`.
options.B: The `paths` field accepts only absolute filesystem paths, so the relative `infra/` prefix prevents any deeper match.
options.C: Rule files must live in a `.claude/rules/` folder beside each module, because the root rules folder cannot reach nested directories.
options.D: Path-scoped rules are triggered only by Read calls, so edits to nested files never load them unless Claude reads the file first.

rationale: Glob semantics decide this: `infra/*.tf` matches .tf files directly under infra/, and `*` never matches a path separator, so modules/vpc/main.tf falls outside it. Using `infra/**/*.tf` (A) covers every depth. Path-scoped rules also load on Write and Edit, not only Read (D). One root `.claude/rules/` folder is enough because the globs are resolved relative to the project (C). Relative patterns are exactly what `paths` expects; absolute paths are not required (B), and the file in infra/ already matched.
evidence: A path-scoped rule loads when Claude reads, writes or edits a file matching its paths globs, relative to the rule's base directory.

task: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team's deploy skill runs the production release script. Twice this week Claude started a deployment on its own right after a developer typed "looks ready to ship"; nobody had typed /deploy. The skill's frontmatter:

```yaml
---
name: deploy
description: Deploy the current branch to production. Use when the change is ready to ship.
allowed-tools: Bash(./scripts/release.sh *)
---
```

Which change stops Claude from starting this skill on its own while still letting developers run /deploy?

options.A: Add `context: fork` so the skill executes in an isolated subagent instead of the main conversation.
options.B: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` so that only a developer typing /deploy can start the skill.
options.C: Delete the `allowed-tools` line so that every release command raises a permission prompt before it runs.
options.D: Reword the description to say the skill should only run when the user explicitly types /deploy.

rationale: The skill is being auto-invoked because its description matches the situation. `disable-model-invocation: true` (B) removes it from Claude's own invocation path and leaves the slash command for people, which is the intended control for side-effect workflows. Removing `allowed-tools` (C) only adds prompts; Claude can still start the skill and a hurried approval ships it. `context: fork` (A) changes where the skill runs, not who may start it. A reworded description (D) is still a probabilistic instruction to the model rather than a setting.
evidence: disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from auto-invoking a skill; use it for workflows with side effects such as /deploy or /commit.

task: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Two tickets are in your queue. Ticket 1: a stack trace shows a NullPointerException at OrderMapper.java:88 when the discount field is absent. Ticket 2: replace moment.js with date-fns across 60 files, where several call sites rely on moment's timezone behavior and the team wants the approach reviewed before any file changes. How should you work each ticket?

options.A: Use plan mode for both tickets, so that every change follows the same review process regardless of size.
options.B: Use direct execution for ticket 1; start ticket 2 in plan mode to map call sites and design the migration, then execute the approved plan.
options.C: Use direct execution for ticket 1; for ticket 2, spawn one subagent per file to migrate in parallel and review the combined diff.
options.D: Use direct execution for both tickets and run the full test suite after each file to catch regressions as they appear.

rationale: Ticket 1 is a clearly scoped fix with a stack trace, so planning adds ceremony without value. Ticket 2 spans many files, has behavioral subtleties and an explicit review requirement, which is what plan mode (read-only exploration, then an approved plan) is for, followed by direct execution of that plan (B). Planning both (A) over-processes the small fix. Executing ticket 2 directly (D) discovers the timezone problems only after files are changed. Parallel per-file subagents (C) edit before anyone has designed or approved the approach, and each subagent lacks the cross-file picture.
evidence: Plan mode suits large multi-file changes with multiple valid approaches; direct execution suits small, well-scoped fixes; plan for investigation then execute.

task: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You ask Claude Code to write a converter from legacy CSV exports to a normalized JSON format. Your prose specification is read differently from run to run: empty quoted fields become null in some runs and empty strings in others, and dates come out in two formats. You need to (1) remove the ambiguity about the expected transformation, and (2) make each refinement round verifiable instead of judged by eye. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Run the converter three times on the sample file and keep whichever output appears most often.
options.B: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in the converter from 1 to 10 after each round and stop at 9 or above.
options.C: Add two or three concrete input and output examples that cover the empty quoted field and the mixed date formats.
options.D: Repeat the empty-field rule three times in the specification so that the instruction carries more weight.
options.E: Write a test suite with the expected outputs first, then iterate by sharing the failing test results with Claude.

rationale: Requirement 1 is an interpretation problem, which concrete input/output examples (C) resolve better than more prose. Requirement 2 is verification, which a test suite written first, with failures fed back each round (E), provides objectively. Repeating the rule (D) is more prose, not clearer prose. Majority-vote over runs (A) hides the ambiguity instead of removing it and still has no definition of correct. Self-reported confidence (B) is an unreliable proxy for whether the output matches the intended transformation.
evidence: Concrete input/output examples fix inconsistent prose interpretation; writing tests first and sharing failures gives test-driven iteration.

task: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Developers have started dismissing every automated review comment, including the security ones. Last month's triage data:

```text
category            posted  dismissed
security                41          3
logic bug               88         11
naming and style       212        187
performance hint        64         58
```

You need to restore trust quickly without losing the categories developers still act on. What should you do first?

options.A: Run each review three times and post only the findings that appear in at least two of the three runs, across all categories.
options.B: Add an instruction to report only findings the model is highly confident about, applying it uniformly to every category in the review prompt.
options.C: Cap every category at ten comments per pull request, ranked by severity, so the volume developers see drops sharply.
options.D: Temporarily disable the naming and performance categories, then rewrite their criteria with explicit report-and-skip rules and examples.

rationale: Dismissal rates show two categories with roughly 90% false positives while security and logic findings are mostly accepted. Pausing the noisy categories keeps the trusted ones credible, and explicit categorical criteria with examples are what actually improve precision (D). A generic 'be confident' instruction (B) does not change what the model considers reportable. Consensus voting (A) multiplies cost and keeps consistent false positives. A volume cap (C) hides real findings along with noise and leaves the bad criteria in place.
evidence: A reviewer asked to find problems will always find something; scope it with explicit criteria (report correctness gaps, skip style) rather than generic filters.

task: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline has Claude Code write a patch with `claude -p`, then continues the same session (`--continue`) with "review the changes you just made" before opening the PR. Over two months, 7 of 40 merged PRs shipped logic errors that this review step had approved. What change most improves the review's ability to catch them?

options.A: Have the same session review each changed file in a separate follow-up turn, so that every file gets its own dedicated look.
options.B: Keep the same session but add a prompt line telling Claude to act as a skeptical senior reviewer who assumes the patch contains bugs.
options.C: Run the review as a separate, fresh `claude -p` invocation that sees only the diff and the review criteria in CLAUDE.md.
options.D: Keep the same session and raise the effort level for the review turn, so Claude reasons for longer about the patch it wrote.

rationale: A session that wrote the code carries the reasoning that produced it, so it tends to justify its own choices rather than challenge them. An independent instance that starts from the diff and the written review criteria (C) is not anchored on that reasoning. A skeptical persona (B), more effort (D) and per-file turns (A) all keep the author's context in the room, so the same blind spots persist.
evidence: A reviewer that has not seen how the code was written, such as a fresh instance, is more effective than the session that generated the changes.

task: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your CI job runs Claude Code on every push to a pull request. Three problems appear: after each new commit the review re-posts comments that developers already addressed or acknowledged; generated unit tests repeat scenarios the suite already covers; and generated tests ignore the team's fixture helpers. You need a fix for each problem. (Select THREE.)

options.A: Include prior review findings in each re-run's context and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
options.B: Supply the existing test files in context so that test generation can skip scenarios that are already covered.
options.C: Document testing standards, what makes a test worth writing, and the available fixtures in CLAUDE.md for the CI run.
options.D: Increase `--max-turns` so that Claude explores more of the repository before it writes each comment or each test.
options.E: Have Claude score each generated test from 1 to 10 and keep only the tests that score 8 or higher in its own rating.

rationale: Duplicate comments come from the re-run not knowing what was already said, so prior findings plus an instruction to report only new or unresolved items (A) address it. Duplicate test scenarios need the existing tests visible (B). Ignoring fixtures and low-value tests is a project-context gap that CLAUDE.md fills for CI-invoked runs (C). More turns (D) adds exploration cost without supplying the missing information. Self-scored quality (E) is an uncalibrated filter that does not know what the suite already covers.
evidence: Include prior findings on re-runs, provide existing tests to avoid duplicates, and document testing standards and fixtures in CLAUDE.md.

task: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills

options.A: Replace the literal with `Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}` in the header and have each developer export their own token in their shell environment.
options.B: Base64-encode the token inside the header value so the credential is not readable in the committed file.
options.C: Keep the literal token, add .mcp.json to .gitignore, and share the file with new developers through the team wiki.
options.D: Remove .mcp.json from the repository and have each developer run `claude mcp add --scope user` with their own token.

rationale: .mcp.json is the project-scoped, version-controlled place for shared server definitions, and it supports `${VAR}` expansion in headers, so the structure can be shared while each person's secret stays in their environment (A). Gitignoring the file (C) removes the automatic sharing. User-scope registration on every laptop (D) works but is manual per developer, which is what the team wants to avoid. Base64 (B) is encoding, not protection, and still commits a shared credential.
evidence: .mcp.json at the project root is shared via version control and supports ${VAR} expansion in command, args, env, url and headers.

task: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines

options.A: The server needs more than the default startup time, so raise `MCP_TIMEOUT` and add `--bare` so the run starts faster and more predictably.
options.B: Environment variable expansion is not supported in HTTP headers, so the literal `${ORDERS_TOKEN}` is rejected and the token must be hard-coded in the file.
options.C: The entry has a `url` but no `type`, so it is skipped; add `"type": "http"` and fail the job when `orders` is absent from `mcp_servers` in the init event.
options.D: Project servers wait for an interactive approval that a CI job cannot give, so run `claude mcp reset-project-choices` before every job.

rationale: A remote entry without `type` is read as stdio, fails validation and is skipped, yet the run continues and exits cleanly; a skipped server is simply absent from `mcp_servers` in the system/init event, which a CI gate can check (C). In `-p` runs project servers load without an approval prompt (D). A longer startup timeout and `--bare` (A) would not help, and `--bare` skips .mcp.json entirely. Header expansion is supported (B), and hard-coding a secret would be a regression.
evidence: A url entry with no type is skipped as a config error; -p runs still exit cleanly, and the system/init event lists the servers that actually loaded.

task: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your team's shared settings block force-pushes. A developer needs one exception for hotfix branches and adds an allow rule locally, but Claude still refuses `git push --force origin hotfix/1.4`.

```text
.claude/settings.json         (committed)
  permissions.deny:  ["Bash(git push --force *)"]
.claude/settings.local.json   (this developer only)
  permissions.allow: ["Bash(git push --force origin hotfix/*)"]
```

Why does the push stay blocked, and what is the correct way to permit the exception?

options.A: Local settings outrank the committed file only for scalar keys, so the allow entry must also be repeated in the committed file itself.
options.B: Pass the allow rule with `--settings`, which sits above both files and so overrides the committed deny rule.
options.C: Rules in the local file load only at session start, so restarting the session applies the allow rule and ends the block on this push.
options.D: Deny is evaluated before allow, so no narrower allow can create an exception; change the shared deny rule through review.

rationale: Permission lists from every scope are combined and evaluated deny first, then ask, then allow, with the first match deciding; specificity does not change that. The exception therefore has to come from narrowing or removing the deny rule where the team owns it (D). Repeating the allow in the committed file (A) would still lose to the deny. Settings changes reload without a restart (C), and the command-line layer (B) merges its list with the others instead of overriding a deny.
evidence: Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins, and an allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule.

task: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. The extraction platform team maintains a validation-retry slash command, a subagent for schema review, a PostToolUse hook that lints JSON schemas, and the configuration for a document-store MCP server. Twelve repositories need the same bundle, and updates must reach all of them without a commit in each repository. How should you distribute it?

options.A: Package everything as a plugin in a team marketplace that each repository enables and updates from.
options.B: Write the standards into a managed-policy CLAUDE.md and describe the setup in prose.
options.C: Install the files into each engineer's `~/.claude/` through an onboarding script so that they apply across projects.
options.D: Copy the `.claude/` directory into every repository, and re-copy it with a script whenever the team changes anything.

rationale: Plugins bundle commands, agents, skills, hooks and MCP servers into one versioned unit that a marketplace distributes and updates, which fits twelve repositories with central updates (A). Copying directories (D) means a commit in every repository for every change and drift between copies. Per-engineer installs in `~/.claude/` (C) are personal, depend on each person running the script, and do not follow the repository. A managed CLAUDE.md (B) can carry instructions but cannot install a hook, subagent or server.
evidence: Plugins bundle commands, agents, skills, hooks and MCP servers and are distributed through marketplaces.

task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. In long sessions the agent sometimes offers the wrong remedy. A trace from one session:

```text
turn 3   customer: "Order 88213, the blender arrived cracked. I paid
                    $129.99 on Oct 3 and want a full refund, not store credit."
turn 12  [history summarized] "Customer reported a damaged item and wants a remedy."
turn 31  agent: "I've applied $129.99 store credit to your account."
```

Which change addresses the root cause?

options.A: Summarize every five turns instead of every twelve, so that less detail is lost between each pair of consecutive summaries.
options.B: Move to a model with a larger context window so that summarization is rarely triggered in typical support sessions, and keep the summary prompt as it is.
options.C: Persist order numbers, amounts, dates and stated preferences in a case-facts block sent with every prompt, outside the summarized history.
options.D: Replace summarization with a sliding window that keeps only the most recent ten turns of the conversation verbatim.

rationale: Progressive summarization turned 'full refund, not store credit' and the exact figures into 'a remedy', and the agent then acted on the vague version. Transactional facts need their own persistent layer that is re-sent each turn and never passes through the summarizer (C). More frequent summaries (A) compress the same facts more often. A sliding window (D) would drop turn 3 outright. A larger context (B) only delays the problem and raises cost without preserving the facts.
evidence: Progressive summarization can lose amounts, dates and customer expectations; persist transactional facts in a case-facts block outside summarized history.

task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The synthesis agent receives 14 subagent reports concatenated in arrival order, about 90,000 tokens, followed by the instructions. Findings from reports 5 through 10 appear in the final answer much less often than findings from reports 1 to 3 and 12 to 14, although every report is accurate. What change most directly addresses this?

options.A: Raise `max_tokens` on the synthesis call so that the final answer has enough room to cover every one of the reports.
options.B: Add an instruction telling the synthesis agent to read the middle reports twice before it starts drafting.
options.C: Open the input with a short summary of key findings, and wrap each report in a labeled section with an explicit header.
options.D: Shuffle the report order on each run and keep whichever answer ends up covering the most reports.

rationale: Models attend most reliably to the beginning and end of a very long input, so findings in the middle are the ones that get dropped. Putting key findings first and giving each report a clear header makes the middle content easier to locate and use (C). The output limit (A) is not the constraint, since the omitted findings were never drafted. Shuffling (D) spreads the loss randomly and adds selection cost. An instruction to read twice (B) cannot change how attention is distributed over the input.
evidence: Put long documents near the top of the prompt, above the query, and structure multi-document input clearly; middle-of-input findings are the ones most often omitted.

task: Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An internal code-search MCP tool returns each hit with the full file contents plus about 40 metadata fields, while the agent only needs path, symbol, line range and a short snippet. After roughly 15 searches in a large repository the session hits its context limit, and the agent must still be able to refer back to every earlier hit. What is the best fix?

options.A: Clear tool results older than the five most recent searches so that old hits stop consuming context in the session.
options.B: Raise `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` so that larger search results fit in the response before any truncation is applied.
options.C: Make the tool return only path, symbol, line range and a short snippet, plus a read-by-id call for full bodies.
options.D: Have the agent write a prose summary of each result after every search and discard the raw output.

rationale: The waste is in what enters context: dozens of fields and entire files that are never used. Trimming the payload at the source keeps every hit referable at a few lines each and lets the agent fetch a full body only when needed (C). A bigger output limit (B) lets more unused data in. Clearing older results (A) breaks the requirement that earlier hits stay available. Prose summaries (D) lose exact paths and line numbers, and the agent still reads the large raw result once before discarding it.
evidence: Tool results accumulate in context; trim verbose outputs to only the relevant fields before they are added to the conversation.

task: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. First-contact resolution is 62% against an 80% target. Logs show two patterns: customers who write "I want to talk to a person" are first walked through an order investigation and many abandon the chat, and the agent confidently improvises when policy is silent, for example a request to match a competitor's price when the policy covers only own-site adjustments. Which two changes address these patterns? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Escalate automatically whenever a sentiment score computed on the customer's message falls below a configured threshold.
options.B: Train a classifier on historical tickets and let it decide which requests skip the agent and go straight to a human queue.
options.C: Escalate immediately when a customer explicitly asks for a human, without first attempting any investigation of the order.
options.D: Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples: policy gaps and exceptions escalate, standard cases such as damage replacements resolve autonomously.
options.E: Have the agent report a confidence score from 1 to 10 for each reply and route the conversation to a human below 7.

rationale: An explicit request for a human is honored immediately (C). Policy gaps are an escalation trigger the agent does not recognize on its own, and explicit criteria with examples teach the boundary between exceptions and routine cases (D). Sentiment (A) measures mood, not case complexity, and frustrated customers with simple issues would be escalated. Self-reported confidence (E) is poorly calibrated, especially when the agent is wrong with confidence. A separate trained classifier (B) adds a component and a training burden without addressing either observed pattern.
evidence: Escalate on explicit customer requests and on policy gaps; sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies for case complexity.

task: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns

options.A: Call lookup_order for all three customer IDs and continue with whichever account has a blender order in its history.
options.B: Escalate to a human agent because the lookup could not identify a unique customer from the information given.
options.C: Ask the customer for another identifier, such as the email or an order number, then repeat the lookup.
options.D: Select C-7790 because its latest order date is the most recent and falls within the phrase "last week" in the message.

rationale: Two accounts in the same city both fit 'last week', so any pick is a guess, and a wrong guess issues or exposes another person's refund. When a lookup returns multiple matches the agent should request an additional identifier and then verify (C). Choosing by recency (D) is a heuristic that fails exactly here. Querying orders for all three (A) pulls data for people who may not be this customer and can still match more than one. Escalating (B) is premature because one simple question resolves the ambiguity.
evidence: When tool results return multiple customer matches, ask for additional identifiers rather than selecting by heuristic.

task: Implement error propagation strategies across multi-agent systems
question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A published report claims that no sources exist on a topic that has abundant coverage. The trace for that subtopic:

```text
coordinator -> web_search_agent: "EU battery recycling targets 2026"
web_search_agent: search API timeout after 30s (attempt 1)
web_search_agent: search API timeout after 30s (attempt 2)
web_search_agent -> coordinator: {"status": "ok", "results": []}
synthesis_agent -> report: "No published sources address EU battery recycling targets."
```

What change to error handling fixes the root cause?

options.A: Return a structured error (failure type, query, partial results, alternatives), distinct from a valid empty result, so the report flags the gap.
options.B: Stop the whole research run as soon as any subagent search times out, and show the exception to the user.
options.C: Instruct the synthesis agent to treat every empty search result as a coverage gap and say so in the report.
options.D: Have the subagent retry until three attempts have failed, then return an empty list marked successful so the coordinator can keep the research run moving.

rationale: The subagent converted an access failure into a successful empty result, so the coordinator and synthesis agent could not tell 'searched, found nothing' from 'could not search'. Structured error context lets the coordinator retry, reroute or annotate the gap (A). Returning empty as success after retries (D) keeps the same silent suppression. Treating all empties as gaps (C) mislabels genuinely empty queries and the synthesis agent still lacks the failure details. Aborting everything (B) discards the other subagents' good work.
evidence: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results; return structured error context so the coordinator can recover; avoid silent suppression.

task: Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. During a three-hour exploration of a 2,000-file monolith, the agent starts answering with "typical service-layer patterns" instead of the actual class names it found earlier, and each search sweep floods the context with raw output. You need to (1) keep earlier findings reliable across context boundaries and compaction, and (2) stop verbose discovery output from consuming the main session's context. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Raise the effort level so that the agent reasons harder about the files and classes it saw earlier in the session.
options.B: Have the agent record key findings (class names, file paths, call relationships) in a scratchpad file it re-reads for later questions.
options.C: Delegate specific questions, such as tracing the refund flow, to subagents that return condensed summaries to the main session.
options.D: Clear the conversation every hour and restart from the original one-line goal so that the session stays fresh and focused.
options.E: Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the entire three-hour exploration fits in a single session.

rationale: Requirement 1 is persistence: a scratchpad file survives compaction and context degradation, and the agent can re-read exact names instead of falling back on generic patterns (B). Requirement 2 is isolation: a subagent absorbs the noisy search output in its own context and returns only a summary (C). A larger window (E) delays degradation without removing it. Restarting hourly (D) throws away the findings. More reasoning effort (A) cannot recover facts that are no longer reliably in context.
evidence: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries; subagents isolate verbose exploration output and return summaries.

task: Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A nightly job extracts 5,000 invoices and posts each one to the ERP. After a crash at invoice 3,100 the operator restarted the job from the beginning, and the ERP now holds 3,100 duplicate postings. How should the pipeline be redesigned so that a crash followed by a rerun is safe?

options.A: Checkpoint the job every 500 invoices and resume from the last checkpoint, accepting a small overlap window.
options.B: Keep a per-invoice status manifest that the job loads on restart, and give ERP writes an idempotency key based on the document ID.
options.C: Run a nightly deduplication job in the ERP that merges postings with the same vendor and the same amount.
options.D: Disable automatic restarts so that an operator inspects the ERP before every rerun of the job begins.

rationale: Safe recovery needs two things: knowing exactly which documents completed (a manifest the coordinator loads on resume) and making each write idempotent so that any replay is harmless (B). Coarse checkpoints (A) leave an overlap window of up to 499 duplicate postings. Vendor-and-amount merging (C) would also merge legitimate repeat invoices. Manual inspection before reruns (D) slows recovery and still offers no guarantee against duplicates.
evidence: Persist agent state to a known location and load a manifest on resume; combine with idempotent writes so a rerun does not duplicate effects.

task: Design human review workflows and confidence calibration
question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. An extraction pipeline reports 97.3% field accuracy against a 95% target, and management proposes auto-approving every extraction with confidence of 0.90 or higher to cut human review by about 90%. Results from the labeled validation set:

```text
doc_type          docs  field_acc  conf>=0.90
invoice_pdf       6200     99.0%        5900
purchase_order    2100     98.0%        1950
handwritten_rcpt   700     80.0%         620
overall           9000     97.3%        8470
```

What should you do before approving the proposal?

options.A: Measure accuracy of high-confidence extractions by document type and field; keep review on segments below target.
options.B: Raise the global confidence threshold to 0.97, which keeps most of the savings while filtering out the weakest extractions.
options.C: Approve the proposal, since the 97.3% overall accuracy already exceeds the 95% target that management set for the pipeline.
options.D: Review a uniform random 2% sample of all auto-approved extractions each month, and approve the rollout if the sample is accurate.

rationale: The aggregate hides a segment problem: handwritten receipts are at 80% while the large invoice and purchase-order populations pull the average up. Accuracy has to be validated by document type and field, ideally with stratified sampling of the high-confidence extractions, before human review is reduced there (A). Relying on the overall figure (C) repeats the aggregate trap. A global threshold (B) was not calibrated per segment and may still pass wrong handwritten fields. A uniform sample (D) would contain too few handwritten receipts to expose the weakness.
evidence: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields; use stratified sampling and segment-level validation before automating.

task: Preserve information provenance and handle uncertainty in multi-source synthesis
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. In final reports, statistics sometimes lose their sources after summarization, and two credible sources give different market sizes ($4.2B and $3.1B) for what looks like the same market. Investigation shows the sources were published two years apart and define the segment differently. You need to (1) keep every claim traceable to its source through synthesis, (2) handle the conflicting figures without hiding either, and (3) stop a time difference from being read as a contradiction. (Select THREE.)

options.A: Keep the figure from the source with the higher relevance score and drop the other figure entirely to keep the report concise.
options.B: Average the two figures into one estimate and cite both sources for the resulting number in the report's summary.
options.C: Require subagents to output structured claim-source mappings (URL, document name, excerpt) that the synthesis agent must preserve and merge.
options.D: Require publication or data-collection dates in every subagent's structured output so synthesis can interpret differences over time.
options.E: Report both figures side by side with their sources and methodological context, marking the finding as contested.

rationale: Traceability survives summarization only if claim-to-source mappings are structured data that synthesis merges rather than prose that gets compressed (C). Conflicting credible figures should be shown with attribution and context, not arbitrarily resolved (E). Dates in the structured output let the reader see that a gap may reflect time or definition rather than error (D). Averaging (B) manufactures a number no source reported. Dropping the lower-ranked source (A) hides a legitimate conflict behind a relevance score.
evidence: Preserve structured claim-source mappings, annotate conflicting statistics with attribution, and require publication or collection dates.

task: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pull-request review job uses the prompt below. Over two weeks developers dismissed 64% of the "comment accuracy" findings but only 9% of the security findings, and several now skim past every review comment. The security category is working well.

```text
You are a code reviewer. For each changed file:
1. Check that comments are accurate.
2. Check for security problems.
3. Check that error handling is adequate.
Be conservative: only report findings you are highly confident about.
```

Which revision most directly reduces the false positives in the comment category?

options.A: Replace item 1 with a rule: report a comment only if the behavior it claims contradicts the code, and skip wording and style remarks.
options.B: Run the comment check as a second pass over the same diff and post only the findings that both passes report.
options.C: Strengthen the last line to say false positives destroy trust, and that the model should stay silent whenever any doubt remains.
options.D: Have the model attach a 0-100 confidence score to every comment finding, and have the pipeline drop any finding scored below 90 before it is posted.

rationale: The fix is a specific, categorical criterion for what counts as a comment finding and what to skip (A). "Be conservative" is already in the prompt and clearly did not help, so a stronger version of the same vague instruction (C) will not either. Self-reported confidence (D) is poorly calibrated and filters by a number rather than by category of issue. Requiring two agreeing passes (B) doubles cost and still lets a vague criterion produce the same wrong findings in both runs.
evidence: Explicit categorical criteria (flag a comment only when its claim contradicts the code) improve precision; generic conservatism or confidence filtering does not.

task: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your automated reviewer reports four categories. Dismissal rates last month were: naming conventions 71%, test-coverage remarks 58%, bugs 12%, security 7%. Developers have started ignoring all reviewer output, and the "high" and "medium" severity labels vary from run to run on similar issues. You want to restore trust quickly and make severity labels stable. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Ask the model to rank findings against each other within each PR so that the top few are always labeled high and the rest medium.
options.B: Switch off the naming and test-coverage categories while you rewrite their criteria and re-measure dismissals on past PRs.
options.C: Add one global instruction telling the model to report only findings it is highly confident about, across all four categories of findings.
options.D: Define every severity level with explicit criteria and a code example, such as high meaning unvalidated input reaches a SQL string.
options.E: Filter out every finding labeled low or medium severity before it is posted, and keep only the high-severity ones in each review.

rationale: Temporarily disabling the two noisy categories (B) restores trust in the accurate ones while the prompts are fixed, and concrete severity definitions with code examples (D) are what make labels consistent. A global confidence instruction (C) is the same vague approach that fails to improve precision. Filtering by severity (E) hides real medium bugs while the label inconsistency stays unsolved.
