Relative ranking inside a PR (A) makes labels depend on what else is in the diff, which is less stable across runs, not more.
evidence: High false-positive categories undermine trust in accurate ones; disable them temporarily, and define severity with explicit criteria and concrete examples.

task: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your invoice extractor uses the strict tool schema below. About 8% of invoices have no purchase order number and 5% have no delivery date. Auditors found that for those invoices the tool returns plausible values such as "PO-0000" and the current date.

```json
{"name": "record_invoice", "strict": true,
 "input_schema": {"type": "object",
  "properties": {
   "vendor": {"type": "string"},
   "po_number": {"type": "string"},
   "delivery_date": {"type": "string", "format": "date"},
   "total": {"type": "number"}},
  "required": ["vendor", "po_number", "delivery_date", "total"],
  "additionalProperties": false}}
```

What schema change best stops the fabrication?

options.A: Keep the schema and add a description telling the model to write "N/A" when the document has no such value.
options.B: Add a minLength of 1 to po_number and a regex pattern to delivery_date so empty or malformed placeholders fail schema validation.
options.C: Keep both fields required and add a post-check that rejects values like PO-0000, then re-ask the model up to three times.
options.D: Declare po_number and delivery_date as string-or-null, keep them in required, and let a missing value come back as null.

rationale: Required non-nullable fields force the model to emit something, so a missing value gets invented. Allowing null (D) gives it an honest way to say the value is absent. Length constraints are not supported in strict schemas and a pattern would still demand a value (B). A sentinel string (A) is still a made-up string that downstream code must special-case. Retrying (C) cannot succeed because the information is not in the document.
evidence: Make fields nullable when the source may not contain them, so the model is not pushed to fabricate values to satisfy required fields.

task: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent files each ticket with a category enum: billing, shipping, returns, product_defect, account_access. In a sample of 300 tickets, 11% were gift-card or loyalty-point issues forced into billing, and 6% were messages too vague to categorize that landed on whichever value the model leaned toward. You want new topics visible for later taxonomy work and vague tickets sent to a human queue. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Add an "other" value paired with a nullable category_detail string where the model describes the topic in a few words.
options.B: Add an "unclear" value reserved in the prompt for ambiguous or underspecified messages, and route it to human review.
options.C: Add a numeric confidence field and drop any ticket scoring under 0.5 from the pipeline, since low-confidence labels are unreliable.
options.D: Expand the enum to 40 granular categories that cover every topic seen in the last year of tickets, so nothing is forced anywhere.
options.E: Change category to a free-text string and map it onto the fixed list with fuzzy matching in the nightly CRM sync job afterward.

rationale: An "other" value with a detail string (A) keeps novel topics honest and collectable, and an "unclear" value (B) gives ambiguous tickets a defined exit to people. A 40-value enum (D) just moves the same forced-fit problem to the long tail and is costly to maintain. Free text plus fuzzy matching (E) throws away the closed set the schema was meant to guarantee. Dropping low-confidence tickets (C) silently loses them and relies on a poorly calibrated number.
evidence: Add enum values like "unclear" for ambiguous cases and "other" plus a detail field for extensible categorization.

task: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your pipeline retries a failed extraction up to three times, appending the validation error to the prompt. Part of last night's retry log is below.

```text
INV-2291 total  err="sum(line_items)=1240.00 != total=1.24"  retry#1 -> ok
INV-3310 date   err="2024-13-04 is not a valid date"          retry#1 -> ok
INV-4407 tax_id err="required field is null"                  retry#1 -> fail
INV-4407 tax_id err="required field is null"                  retry#2 -> fail
INV-4407 tax_id err="required field is null"                  retry#3 -> fail
note: INV-4407 text reads "Tax ID: see attached Schedule B" (no attachment uploaded)
```

Which kind of failure should the pipeline stop retrying and send to a human-review queue?

options.A: Quantities that were placed in the unit-price field instead of the quantity field in a multi-column table
options.B: Line items that fail to sum to the stated total because a decimal separator in the document was misread
options.C: Dates that fail validation because the day and the month were swapped when the model read an ambiguous format
options.D: Required values that are null because the document cites an attachment that was never supplied

rationale: Retry with error feedback works for format and structural mistakes where the answer is in the document (A, B, C all show or imply a successful retry in the log). It cannot work when the information is simply absent: the tax ID lives in an attachment that was not provided (D), as three identical failures show. Those documents should go to review or trigger a request for the missing file.
evidence: Retries are ineffective when the required information is absent from the source; they work for format mismatches and structural errors.

task: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your extraction tool uses strict schemas, so every response parses. Even so, 3% of invoices reach downstream systems with line items that do not add up to the stated total, and in some of those the printed invoice itself is inconsistent. Finance wants these caught automatically without manually checking the other 97%. What design change achieves this?

options.A: Enable strict mode on the nested line_items objects so the grammar guarantees the arithmetic is consistent.
options.B: Add minimum and maximum constraints to the total field so that out-of-range sums are rejected while the model generates.
options.C: Extract stated_total as printed plus a calculated_total from the line items, add a conflict_detected flag, and route mismatches to review.
options.D: Instruct the model to double-check that the line items sum to the total, and rerun any invoice that still fails up to five times.

rationale: Strict schemas remove syntax errors but not semantic ones such as totals that disagree. Extracting both totals and flagging the conflict (C) turns the discrepancy into data the pipeline can route, including cases where the source is itself wrong. Numeric range limits are not supported by the grammar and would not check a sum anyway (B). A prompt reminder with reruns (D) cannot fix a source that is inconsistent. Strict mode (A) is already on and guarantees shape, not arithmetic.
evidence: Strict schemas do not prevent semantic errors; extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and add conflict_detected to flag discrepancies.

task: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent labels each inbound message with one of nine intents before choosing tools. The prompt already defines every intent clearly, yet in a 200-message audit about 35% of messages like "the blender arrived cracked and I want my money back, not a new one" flipped between damage_claim and refund_request across runs. Which change most reliably improves consistency?

options.A: Add 25 more examples of unambiguous messages so that each of the nine intents has at least three typical cases to learn from.
options.B: Label every message twice and accept the label only when both runs agree, escalating the rest.
options.C: Ask the agent to rate its confidence from 1 to 10 on each label, and send the low-rated messages to a human agent for review.
options.D: Add 3-4 few-shot examples of borderline messages with a one-line reason for picking one intent over its rival.

rationale: The definitions are already clear; what is missing is demonstrated judgment at the boundary. A few targeted examples with the reasoning for the choice (D) teach the model how to resolve this kind of ambiguity and generalize to new cases. More typical examples (A) do not touch the ambiguous region. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated. Double labeling (B) detects disagreement but does not remove it, and sends a third of the traffic to escalation.
evidence: Create 2-4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios that show why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.

task: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your /gen-tests command writes unit tests for TypeScript modules. The command file already has detailed written instructions, but output is inconsistent: some runs cover only the happy path, others skip branches that return early, and test names follow no pattern. You will add few-shot examples to the command so that branch gaps get covered and reviewers get one predictable layout. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Include one example for every module in the repository so the model has seen all of the code it could be asked to test.
options.B: Show the exact layout wanted in every example: a describe block per function and names in the form "should X when Y".
options.C: Include 2-4 examples on modules with early returns and error branches, showing the test for each branch and why it is needed.
options.D: Write each example as a complete suite of 20 or more tests so that every possible pattern appears at least once.
options.E: Use one happy-path example only, because the written instructions already describe the edge cases in words.

rationale: Examples that demonstrate branch-level gaps with the reasoning (C) address the skipped-branch problem, and examples that all use the required layout (B) fix naming and structure. One example per module (A) is unfocused and bloats the command. Very long suites (D) bury the pattern. A happy-path-only example (E) reinforces the very behavior that is going wrong.
evidence: A few targeted examples can demonstrate ambiguous-case handling such as branch-level coverage gaps and the desired output format.

task: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The synthesis subagent must return findings as JSON with a claim, a source URL, and a supporting quote, which the report builder validates. A developer enabled citations on the source documents and an output_config.format JSON schema in the same request, and every call now fails with a 400. The builder only needs claim, URL, and a quote it can verify. What is the best fix?

options.A: Keep both settings and retry with exponential backoff and jitter, since a 400 on a large request usually indicates transient capacity pressure.
options.B: Turn the schema off, keep citations, and tell the model to reply with only a JSON object and no other text.
options.C: Turn citations off, add source_url and supporting_quote fields to the schema, and verify each quote against the source text in code.
options.D: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so the model continues in JSON while citations stay enabled.

rationale: Citations cannot be combined with a JSON-schema output format, and a 400 is not retryable (A). Since the builder only needs a verifiable quote, putting source_url and supporting_quote in the schema and verifying the quote programmatically (C) keeps guaranteed structure. Asking for JSON only with citations (B) tends to produce few or no citations and loses schema enforcement. Assistant prefill (D) is rejected on current models.
evidence: Citations are incompatible with output_config.format (400); JSON-only prompts can yield few citations; prefill is not supported on current models.

task: Design efficient batch processing strategies
question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Every night you re-score 20,000 closed tickets for QA with the Message Batches API, and supervisors read the results at 8 a.m. Last night the job submitted fine, but results were joined to the ticket table by line position and 1,900 tickets received the wrong score. Separately, 140 requests came back errored or expired. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Resubmit the whole batch of 20,000 so that every ticket is scored by the same run.
options.B: Collect only the errored and expired requests and submit them again in a new batch once the causes are fixed.
options.C: Poll the batch every second so each result is read as soon as its request finishes.
options.D: Rely on the results file matching submission order, and sort both sides by timestamp before joining.
options.E: Give each request a custom_id equal to its ticket ID and join results to tickets by that ID.

rationale: Batch results can come back in any order, so correlation must use custom_id (E) rather than position (D). Only failed or expired requests need another try, and a targeted resubmission (B) keeps the cost saving, while rerunning everything (A) pays again for 19,860 good results. Results are available only once the batch has ended, so aggressive polling (C) gains nothing.
evidence: Batch results may be returned in any order; use custom_id to correlate, and resubmit only failed requests.

task: Design efficient batch processing strategies
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A nightly job generates unit tests for 600 modules: one request per module writes the tests, your CI runner executes them, and each failing suite gets one repair attempt using the failure output. Results are needed by 7 a.m., and leadership wants the batch discount on both steps. How should you structure the repair step?

options.A: Send the repair step as real-time calls for all 600 modules, since a batch cannot take a second turn or run a tool for you.
options.B: Run generation as one batch, run tests in your own job, then batch only the failing modules with their output.
options.C: Give each batch request a run_tests tool so that the model executes the suite and repairs failures inside the same request.
options.D: Put the generation prompt and a repair prompt for each module in one request as consecutive user turns, in a single batch.

rationale: Each batch request is an independent single pass: it cannot pause while your runner executes tests and then continue. Chaining two batches around your own test run (B) keeps the 50% saving on both steps and meets a morning deadline. A client-side tool cannot be executed mid-request in a batch (C). The repair prompt cannot see test output that does not exist yet at submission time (D). Real-time calls for all 600 modules (A) gives up the discount, and most modules will not need repair.
evidence: Batch requests are independent and cannot execute client tools mid-request; chain batches around the step your own system runs.

task: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your agent files issues through a create_issue tool whose schema defines priority as an enum (p0 to p3) and estimate_points as an integer. About 3% of calls arrive with priority "urgent" or estimate_points "5 pts", and the issue API rejects them. The agent runs on Sonnet 5.5. Which change guarantees that tool inputs conform to the schema?

options.A: Add several few-shot examples of valid create_issue calls to the system prompt.
options.B: Set strict: true on create_issue, with every field in required and additionalProperties set to false.
options.C: Set tool_choice to the named create_issue tool so the model is forced to produce a call that conforms to the schema.
options.D: Set output_config.format to the same schema so that the model's final answer is validated against it as well.

rationale: Strict tool use constrains the generated tool input to the schema (B). Forcing a tool (C) does not validate content and is rejected on Sonnet 5.5 anyway. output_config.format shapes the model's final reply, not tool-call arguments (D). Examples (A) improve the odds but remain probabilistic, so they cannot guarantee conformance.
evidence: Strict tool use (strict: true with additionalProperties false and required) guarantees schema-valid tool inputs; forced tool_choice is not supported on current models.

task: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Traces show the agent picks the wrong one of the two tools below in about 30% of calls. Both calls succeed, but the output has the wrong shape for the task.

```json
{"name": "analyze_content",
 "description": "Analyzes content and returns the key information.",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"content": {"type": "string"}}}}
{"name": "analyze_document",
 "description": "Analyzes a document and returns the key information.",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"document": {"type": "string"}}}}
```

Web results arrive as HTML text and papers arrive as extracted PDF text. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Rename them to extract_web_results and extract_paper_claims, and rewrite each description with its input, output, and when not to use it.
options.B: Add a code-level router that checks each input for HTML tags and calls the matching tool itself.
options.C: Merge the two into a single analyze tool with a source_type parameter that the model sets on every call.
options.D: Add few-shot examples to the coordinator prompt showing which tool to call for web pages and which for papers.

rationale: The two descriptions are nearly identical, so selection is a coin flip. Distinct names and descriptions that state the input, the output, and the boundary (A) fix the cause. Examples (D) work around a poor interface and add prompt weight. A merged tool (C) pushes the same ambiguity into a parameter the model must guess. A router (B) adds a deterministic layer that duplicates a decision the descriptions should make clear.
evidence: Overlapping, near-identical descriptions cause misrouting; rename tools and rewrite descriptions to differentiate purpose, inputs, outputs, and boundaries.

task: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The descriptions of get_customer and lookup_order were recently rewritten with clear boundaries, and the customer ID is already verified at session start. Even so, the agent calls get_customer for order-status questions in about 20% of conversations. Part of the system prompt is below.

```text
You are a support agent for Northwind.
- Be concise and friendly.
- Treat any message that mentions an order as a customer-account question.
- Escalate when a customer asks for a manager.
```

What is the best fix?

options.A: Add six few-shot examples to the system prompt in which an order-status question goes straight to lookup_order without a customer lookup.
options.B: Reword the second bullet so it stops tying order mentions to account handling, since it overrides the tool descriptions.
options.C: Rename get_customer to fetch_account_profile so that its name no longer matches the word "customer" in the prompt.
options.D: Add disable_parallel_tool_use so the agent can call only one tool per turn and must choose more carefully.

rationale: System prompt wording can create keyword-driven tool associations that override even good descriptions. The second bullet links any order mention to the customer-account path, so fixing that instruction (B) removes the cause. Examples (A) would fight an instruction that stays in place. A rename (C) is cosmetic and leaves the misleading rule. Limiting parallel calls (D) does not change which tool is chosen.
evidence: Keyword-sensitive instructions in the system prompt can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions.

task: Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team's MCP server exposes a run_tests tool, and the agent keeps retrying calls that cannot succeed. All three of the server's failure paths return the same payload:

```json
{"isError": true, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Operation failed"}]}
```

The paths are: the CI runner is busy (clears within a minute), the requested test path does not exist in the repo, and the caller's token lacks access to the protected suite. Which redesign lets the agent choose between retrying, correcting its input, and stopping?

options.A: Return an empty test report with isError false for the two non-transient paths so the agent stops looping.
options.B: Retry every failure inside the server three times and return only the final failure, so the agent never sees a transient error.
options.C: Put numeric codes such as 503, 404, and 403 in the message text and document their meaning in the project's CLAUDE.md file.
options.D: Keep isError true and add errorCategory (transient, validation, permission), an isRetryable flag, and what to change.

rationale: A uniform "Operation failed" hides the information needed to recover. Structured metadata (D) separates transient, validation, and permission failures and says whether retrying is worthwhile. Bare codes in text with a separate documentation file (C) is fragile and not machine-readable. Server-side retries of everything (B) waste time on errors that can never succeed. An empty successful report (A) disguises failures as results.
evidence: Return isError with structured metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable, description) so agents can tell transient, validation, and permission errors apart.

task: Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The search subagent's tool returns an empty list with no error flag both when a query truly matches nothing and when the search index times out. The coordinator has been writing "no relevant sources exist" into reports after outages. You are redesigning error handling between the tool, the subagent, and the coordinator. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Return an empty list with a warning inside the text and let the coordinator infer whether the search was really attempted.
options.B: Propagate every tool error to the coordinator immediately so that one component owns all recovery decisions.
options.C: Let the subagent retry transient failures with backoff, and report only unresolved ones with the query and any partial results.
options.D: Return isError true with a transient category and isRetryable on timeouts, and a normal empty result when nothing matches.
options.E: Raise the index timeout to 120 seconds so that timeouts no longer produce empty responses in the first place.

rationale: An access failure and a valid empty result must look different, which the error flag and category in (D) provide. Handling transient errors inside the subagent and escalating only what it cannot resolve, with context and partial results (C), keeps the coordinator informed without noise. A warning buried in text (A) is not a reliable signal. Escalating everything (B) floods the coordinator with errors the subagent could fix. A longer timeout (E) treats the symptom, and outages would still look like empty results.
evidence: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results; recover from transient errors locally and propagate only unresolved errors with partial results.

task: Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A teammate committed this .mcp.json so the whole team gets the Jira server. Security has flagged the committed token.

```json
{"mcpServers": {"jira": {
  "type": "http",
```

Which change keeps a single shared definition and removes the secret from version control?

task: Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your agent works against a 400-table analytics warehouse and spends its first several tool calls each session listing and describing tables. Separately, one engineer wants to try an unvetted community MCP server that parses query plans, without it appearing for teammates. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Add the experimental server to the committed .mcp.json on a feature branch and ask teammates not to approve it.
options.B: Add a list_tables tool to the shared server and instruct the agent to call it first in every session.
options.C: Expose the schema catalog from the shared server as an MCP resource so tables and columns are visible without exploratory calls.
options.D: Paste the full 400-table schema into the project CLAUDE.md so it loads at the start of every session.
options.E: Add the experimental server at local or user scope so its configuration stays in ~/.claude.json and out of the repository.

rationale: MCP resources are designed to expose content catalogs such as database schemas so the agent can see what exists without exploratory calls (C). A personal or experimental server belongs in local or user scope, which is private to that developer (E). A 400-table dump in CLAUDE.md (D) permanently consumes context and goes stale. A list_tables tool (B) still costs a call each session. A committed .mcp.json (A) puts the experiment in front of the whole team.
evidence: MCP resources expose content catalogs like database schemas; personal or experimental servers go in local/user scope, shared ones in project .mcp.json.

task: Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your team added an MCP server with a find_references tool that resolves symbol usage through the language server, handling aliases, re-exports, and renamed imports. Traces show the agent still uses built-in Grep for most reference searches and misses re-exported symbols. The tool's current description reads "Finds references." What is the best first step?

options.A: Rewrite the description: it resolves aliases and re-exports, returns file and line locations, and should be preferred over Grep for symbols.
options.B: Add find_references to the permission allow list so that its calls run without interrupting approval prompts each time.
options.C: Add a deny rule for Grep so the agent has no alternative to find_references when it searches for symbols.
options.D: Move the server's configuration from project scope to user scope so that it outranks the built-in tools.

rationale: The agent chooses tools by their descriptions, and a two-word description gives no reason to prefer the MCP tool over a familiar built-in (A). Denying Grep (C) removes a tool that is still right for plain text searches. Permissions (B) control approval, not selection. Scope (D) controls where a server loads and does not rank tools against built-ins.
evidence: Enhance MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs so the agent does not prefer built-in tools like Grep over more capable MCP tools.

task: Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively
question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You ask Claude to change the retry count in one of three identical lines (retries: 3) in a 900-line config file. The Edit call fails because the old text matches more than one location, and you want only the retries line in the payments block changed. What is the most reliable next step?

options.A: Use Bash to run sed over the whole file, then read the git diff to find out which lines were changed.
options.B: Use Write to recreate the whole file without first reading its current contents from disk.
options.C: Re-run Edit with a longer old_string that includes neighboring lines unique to the payments block.
options.D: Re-run Edit with replace_all so every match is updated, then revert the other two lines by hand afterward.

rationale: Edit requires old_string to match exactly once, and adding surrounding lines that pin down the intended occurrence (C) makes it unique while leaving everything else untouched. replace_all (D) changes all three and creates cleanup work. A global sed (A) has the same all-match problem and is a blunter tool. Writing the file blind (B) risks dropping the other 899 lines; if Edit cannot be made unique, Read followed by Write is the fallback.
evidence: Edit's old_string must appear exactly once; supply more surrounding context to pin one occurrence, or use replace_all to change all.

task: Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively
question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are writing guidance for a codebase-exploration agent that uses the Agent SDK's built-in tools. Which pairings of task and tool are correct? (Select THREE.)

options.A: Listing every file that matches **/*.test.tsx: Glob with that pattern.
options.B: Finding every caller of parseInvoice across the repository: Grep for the identifier.
options.C: Listing every file named like *.test.tsx: Grep, with "test.tsx" as the search pattern over file contents.
options.D: Changing one function in a large file: Read to see the current text, then Edit with a unique snippet.
options.E: Changing one line in a 2,000-line file: Write with the complete new contents so nothing is missed.

rationale: Grep searches file contents, so it finds call sites (B). Glob matches file paths by pattern (A). A targeted change is best done by reading the file and then using Edit with a unique snippet (D). Grep over contents (C) does not match file names. Rewriting a 2,000-line file to change one line (E) is wasteful and risks accidental changes elsewhere.
evidence: Grep searches file contents, Glob matches file paths, Read loads files, and Edit makes targeted changes using unique text.

task: Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice
question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your pipeline receives mixed documents and offers three extraction tools. It used tool_choice any to guarantee a tool call, and after a move to Sonnet 5.5 every request fails with a 400.

```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[extract_invoice, extract_receipt, extract_contract],
    tool_choice={"type": "any"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc_text}],
)
```

What is the right fix that keeps schema-valid structured output?

options.A: Use tool_choice auto with strict: true on all three tools, tell the model to call one, and handle a reply with no tool_use.
options.B: Set tool_choice to none and ask for a JSON object in plain text, validating it with a schema library afterward.
options.C: Catch the 400 and resend without tools, then parse the JSON in the text reply with a regular expression.
options.D: Change tool_choice to the named extract_invoice tool, and run the other two extraction tools in a second pass when they are needed.

rationale: Forced tool use (any or a named tool) is not supported on Sonnet 5.5; the supported pattern is auto plus an instruction naming the expected behavior, strict: true to guarantee valid inputs, and handling the case where no tool is called (A). A named tool (D) is also forced and also returns 400. Dropping tools and parsing text with a regex (C) gives up schema enforcement. Plain-text JSON (B) removes the guarantee that the tool-based design was meant to provide.
evidence: Forced tool_choice (any or tool) returns 400 on current models; use auto with strict tool use or structured outputs for guaranteed schema-valid results.

task: Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice
question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The coordinator and its four subagents share one registry of 19 tools (web search, fetch, PDF parsing, citation lookup, database queries, report templating, and more). Traces show the synthesis subagent running its own web searches and the report subagent calling database queries, and wrong-tool errors rose from 4% to 17% as tools were added. Which change best addresses the cause?

options.A: Upgrade the subagents to a larger model so they can reason reliably over all 19 tools at once.
options.B: Combine related tools into six broader tools that take a mode parameter, to shrink the registry.
options.C: Add a line to each subagent's prompt listing the specific tools that this subagent must not use.
options.D: Give each subagent only the 4-5 tools its role needs, plus at most one narrow cross-role tool

rationale: Selection quality degrades as the tool count grows, and agents tend to misuse tools outside their specialty. Scoping each subagent to its role's tools (D) removes both problems at once. A prompt prohibition (C) is probabilistic and keeps the tools visible. Merged mode-based tools (B) trade clear boundaries for parameters the model must guess. A bigger model (A) spends more without removing the unneeded choices.
evidence: Too many tools degrades selection; give each agent only the tools its role needs, with limited cross-role tools for high-frequency needs.

task: Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice
question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your PR review job connects a GitHub MCP server that exposes 40 tools, including merge_pull_request and delete_branch. The job only needs to read the diff and post review comments. Last week a prompt-injected code comment made the agent attempt a merge, which branch protection blocked. Which is the most robust change?

options.A: Allow only the read and comment tools the review needs by name, and deny the rest of the server's tools in the job's permission rules.
options.B: Add a system prompt rule that the reviewer must never merge, close, or delete anything in the repository.
options.C: Add a second Claude call that reviews each planned tool call and approves it before it runs.
options.D: Scan each tool call for names containing merge or delete and cancel the matches in a wrapper script.

rationale: The safest tool is one the agent does not have. Restricting the job to the few tools it needs by explicit name, enforced by permission rules outside the model (A), also cuts the tool count from 40 to a handful. A prompt rule (B) is probabilistic and injection can override it. A second model call (C) adds cost and can be fooled by the same injected text. A name-based blocklist (D) is brittle: it misses tools with other names, such as force-pushing or editing branch settings.
evidence: Scope tools to what the role needs and enforce restrictions with permission rules outside the model; prompts alone are probabilistic.
